item.research_question: How can a quinary refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) be designed to exhibit high thermal stability and superior resistance to extreme irradiation environments (specifically heavy ion irradiation and helium implantation) without precipitation or grain coarsening?
item.material_system: Quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA; specific compositions: W29.4Ta42Cr5.0V16.1Hf7.5 (thin film) and W31Ta34Cr5.0V27Hf3.0 (thick film)
item.processing_route: Magnetron-sputtering deposition from metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature, 3 mTorr pressure, and no bias voltage; thin films (100 nm) on NaCl substrates and thick films (3 µm) on W substrates; in situ TEM annealing at 1173 K for 10 minutes; ex situ irradiation at 1073 K.
item.test_conditions: In situ TEM ion irradiation at 1173 K using 1-MeV Kr+2 and 16 keV He+ (dual-beam) to 8.5 dpa and ~9% He; single-beam 16 keV He+ implantation to ~9%; ex situ 400 keV Ar+2 irradiation to 10 dpa at 1073 K; nanoindentation at 200 nm depth; APT analysis.
key_findings: Average grain size of as-deposited sample was 24.5 ± 1.3 nm, increasing to 26.3 ± 1.1 nm after annealing at 1173 K.
Grain refinement occurred during dual-beam irradiation, with average grain size dropping to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after ~94 mins.
No dislocation loops were detected even after 8.5 dpa and 9.13% He implantation during dual-beam experiments.
Cavity formation saturated after 5 dpa, with total volume change of ~0.3% after 8.45 dpa and higher He percentages.
Unirradiated sample hardness was 13.25 GPa, increasing to 16.25 GPa after annealing and 20 GPa after irradiation.
Hf segregates to grain boundaries after annealing but depletes from grain boundaries during irradiation.
No precipitation was observed in irradiated samples, unlike the quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA which showed Cr-V precipitation.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the high irradiation resistance to a combination of factors: high density of stable grain boundaries causing grain refinement via cascade effects (where cascades larger than grain size break grains), chemical complexity altering defect recombination rates, and a decrease in the order-disorder transition temperature (ODTT) which promotes homogenization and prevents precipitation. The absence of dislocation loops is linked to high interstitial-vacancy recombination and a rough energy landscape for He migration that favors smaller, uniform bubble nucleation.
item.limitations: The authors acknowledge that the study used ion irradiation rather than neutron irradiation, stating that 'further work (e.g., response to neutron irradiation) is necessary to advance the technology readiness level (TRL) of this material'. They also note that different compositions can have different SRO parameters and segregation behaviors, and that tensile measurements on coarse grain and bulk forms are needed.
item.future_work: The authors propose that 'tensile measurements should follow on coarse grain and bulk forms' and that 'the effect of SRO on the mechanical behavior of future RHEA in extreme environments is another research topic to be further explored'. They also suggest the design methodology can be used to 'devise and synthesize new RHEAs for different applications'.
quotes: Grain refinement occurred, and the average grain size dropped to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after a total irradiation time of ~94 mins.
Dislocation loops were not detected even after 8.5 dpa and at 9.13% He implantation during the dual-beam experiment.
The irradiation response to loop and cavity formation in W-based RHEAs was attributed to high interstitial-vacancy recombination.
